original_question: Which hereditary syndrome is characterized by hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps, trichilemmomas, and is associated with a PTEN gene mutation on chromosome 10q23.3, as opposed to a mutation in the STK11 gene on chromosome 19?

final_qi.question: Which hereditary syndrome is characterized by hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps, trichilemmomas, and is associated with a PTEN gene mutation on chromosome 10q23.3, as opposed to a mutation in the STK11 gene on chromosome 19?
final_qi.search_keyword: hereditary syndrome hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps PTEN gene mutation chromosome 10q23.3
final_qi.long_answer: Cowden syndrome is the hereditary syndrome characterized by hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps and trichilemmomas, and it is associated with a mutation in the PTEN gene on chromosome 10q23.3. This syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and predisposes individuals to various benign and malignant tumors, including those in the thyroid, breast, kidney, and endometrium. It is distinct from other polyposis syndromes like Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, which is linked to mutations in the STK11 gene on chromosome 19.

- Wikipedia: Information about: Cowden syndrome
Section: Signs and symptoms
Females have an elevated risk of developing endometrial cancers, which is highest for those under the age of 50.[4] Currently, it is not clear whether uterine leiomyomata (fibroids) or congenital genitourinary abnormalities occur at an increased rate in Cowden syndrome patients as compared to the general population.[4] The occurrence of multiple testicular lipomas, or testicular lipomatosis, is a characteristic finding in male patients with Cowden syndrome.[4] Polyps are extremely common as they are found in about 95% of Cowden syndrome patients undergoing a colonoscopy.[4] They are numerous ranging from a few to hundreds, usually of the hamartomatous subtype, and distributed across the colon as well as other areas within the gastrointestinal tract.[4][12] Other types of polyps that may be encountered less frequently include ganglioneuromatous, adenomatous, and lymphoid polyps.[12] Diffuse glycogenic acanthosis of the esophagus is another gastrointestinal manifestation associated with Cowden syndrome.[4] Patients are also at an increased risk for colorectal cancer with an estimated lifetime risk at 9%.[6]
Section: Genetics
Cowden syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion.[16][page needed] Germline mutations in PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog), a tumor suppressor gene, are found in up to 80% of Cowden's patients.[12] Several other hereditary cancer syndromes, such as Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba syndrome, have been associated with mutations in the PTEN gene as well.[17][page needed]  PTEN negatively regulates the cytoplasmic receptor tyrosine kinase pathway, which is responsible for cell growth and survival, and also functions to repair errors in DNA.[16][12] Thus, in the absence of this protein, cancerous cells are more likely to develop, survive, and proliferate.[12] Recently, it was discovered that germline heterozygous mutations in SEC23B, a component of coat protein complex II vesicles secreted from the endoplasmic reticulum, are associated with Cowden syndrome.[18] A possible interplay between PTEN and SEC23B has recently been suggested, given emerging evidence of each having a role in ribosome biogenesis, but this has not been conclusively determined.[19]
